people.name: Taking Children Seriously
people.text: The parenting approach behind the book, which says children's wishes should be taken as seriously as adults' and that nobody need lose a conflict.

people.name: Creativity
people.text: The capacity to find new solutions, which the authors argue can resolve conflicts between parent and child so that everyone gets what they want.

people.name: Coercion
people.text: Forcing a child to do something against their will, which the authors argue harms learning and the trust between parent and child, even when well meant.

context.title: A normative proposal
context.text: Stupple argues that children's reasons deserve serious engagement. His examples illustrate the proposal; they do not independently establish every claim about outcomes.
context.takeaway: Separate the ethical claim from the empirical claim.

passages.quote: Eating may be the most personal human experience.

context.title: Learning through criticism
context.text: The book draws on critical rationalism: ideas improve through problems, proposals, and correction. It extends this account into family relationships.
context.takeaway: Examine each step from knowledge theory to practice.

opening: A child wants to keep playing; a parent says it is bedtime. The parent can end the dispute by exercising authority, but Aaron Stupple asks what has actually been resolved. Drawing on life with his five children, he argues for abandoning rules in favour of finding solutions that take the child's reasons seriously. His proposal reaches into food, screens, and the daily negotiations of family life, challenging the assumption that preparing someone for independence requires years of making their choices for them.
